q: What is the punishment for murder under BNS section 103?
answer:
Under BNS § 103, whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. [BNS § 103]

Note: IPC § 302 is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 103.

q: What is the punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 105 of the BNS?
answer:
Under section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder is imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death. If the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, or to cause such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and with fine.

[Cited from: BNS § 105]

Note: IPC § 304 is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 105.

q: What is the minimum punishment for rape under BNS section 64?
answer:
Under BNS § 64, the minimum punishment for rape is rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life. [BNS § 64]

Note: IPC § 376 is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 64.

q: What is the punishment for theft under section 303 of the BNS?
answer:
Under section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the punishment for theft is as follows:

- For the first conviction, the offender shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
- For second or subsequent convictions, the offender shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and with fine. [BNS § 303(2)]

Note: IPC § 378 is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 303.

q: What is the punishment for cheating under BNS 318?
answer:
Under [BNS § 318], the punishment for cheating varies based on the circumstances:

1. For general cheating, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
2. For cheating with the knowledge that it will cause wrongful loss to a person whose interest the cheater was bound to protect, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
3. For cheating that involves inducing the delivery of property, making, altering, or destroying a valuable security, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and also liable to fine.

These provisions outline the different penalties depending on the severity and context of the cheating.

q: What is the punishment for criminal intimidation under BNS section 351?
answer:
Under BNS § 351, the punishment for criminal intimidation is as follows:

- Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
- If the threat involves causing death or grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, or an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or imputing unchastity to a woman, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
- If the threat is made anonymously or with precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to the punishment provided for the offence under sub-section (1).

[Reference: BNS § 351]

Note: IPC § 503 is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 351.

q: Under BNS section 85, what is the punishment for a husband who subjects a woman to cruelty?
answer:
Under BNS § 85, a husband who subjects a woman to cruelty is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and is also liable to fine. [BNS § 85]

Note: IPC § 498A is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BNS § 85.

q: What is the punishment under IPC 498A?
answer: Under the repealed section [IPC § 498A], the punishment for a husband or a relative of the husband who subjects a woman to cruelty is imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine.

q: What does BNSS section 482 provide?
answer: BNSS section 482 provides a procedure for a person apprehending arrest on a non-bailable offence to apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction to be released on bail if arrested. The court may grant such a direction with conditions, including availability for police interrogation, non-interference with witnesses, prohibition from leaving India without permission, and other conditions as specified. If the person is arrested and prepared to give bail, they will be released on bail. This section does not apply to cases involving offences under specific sections of the BNS. [BNSS § 482]

q: What is anticipatory bail and which section covers it?
answer: Anticipatory bail is provided under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, specifically covered by [BNSS § 482]. This section allows a person to apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction to be released on bail if they have reason to believe they may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence.

q: Which BNSS section deals with information about a cognizable offence, the FIR?
answer: The section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 that deals with information about a cognizable offence and the First Information Report (FIR) is [BNSS § 173]. This section outlines the procedures for reporting cognizable offences to the police and how such information should be recorded.

q: When can the police arrest without a warrant under BNSS section 35?
answer:
Under [BNSS § 35], a police officer may arrest without a warrant if any of the following conditions are met:
1. The person commits a cognizable offence in the presence of a police officer.
2. A reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that the person has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years, provided the arrest is necessary to prevent further offences, for proper investigation, to prevent evidence tampering, to prevent inducements, or to ensure the person's presence in court.
3. The person is credible information has been received that they have committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years or with death sentence, and the police officer has reason to believe they have committed the said offence.
4. The person has been proclaimed as an offender by a State Government.
5. The person is in possession of stolen property and is reasonably suspected of having committed an offence with reference to such property.
6. The person obstructs a police officer while in the execution of their duty, has escaped, or attempts to escape from lawful custody.
7. The person is reasonably suspected of being a deserter from any of the Armed Forces of the Union.
8. The person has been concerned in, or is reasonably suspected of having been concerned in, any act committed at any place out of India which, if committed in India, would be a cognizable offence.

These conditions must be satisfied, and the police officer must record their reasons in writing for the arrest.

q: What is the longest period a magistrate can authorise detention in police custody under BNSS 187?
answer:
Under [BNSS § 187(3)], the longest period a magistrate can authorise detention in police custody is:

- Ninety days for offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term of ten years or more.
- Sixty days for other offences.

These periods can be extended further only if adequate grounds exist, but the total period cannot exceed the specified limits.

q: What is the punishment for cheque bounce under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
answer: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the punishment for cheque bounce includes imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or both. [NIA § 138]

q: Within how many days must the payee send a notice after the cheque is returned unpaid, under section 138 NI Act?
answer: The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must send a notice within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid. [NIA § 138]

q: What presumption does section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act create?
answer: Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, creates a presumption that the holder of a cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, unless the contrary is proved. [NIA § 139]

q: Who is liable when a company commits an offence under section 138, according to section 141 of the NI Act?
answer: According to section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, if a company commits an offence under section 138, both the company and any person who was in charge of and responsible for the company's business at the time of the offence are liable. However, this liability does not apply if the person proves they were unaware of the offence or had exercised due diligence to prevent it. [NIA § 141]

q: Is electronic evidence admissible under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, and under which section?
answer:
Yes, electronic evidence is admissible under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. This is governed by [BSA § 63].

The section states that any information contained in an electronic record, if certain conditions are satisfied, can be deemed a document and admitted as evidence without further proof of the original.

Note: IEA § 82 is repealed and no longer in force.

q: What was section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act about?
answer:
Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, dealt with the admissibility of electronic records. It provided that electronic records, when produced by a computer, could be admitted as evidence without the need to produce the original, provided certain conditions were met. These conditions included regular use of the computer for the relevant activities, regular feeding of information into the computer, and the computer operating properly during the relevant period. [IEA § 65B]

Note: IEA § 65B is repealed and no longer in force; the corresponding provision is BSA § 63.

q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?
answer: The Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621, held that the procedure prescribed by the state under Article 21 must be fair and reasonable. The court also noted that the principles of natural justice must be read into the concerned provisions, and that a person has a right to be heard before a final order is passed, even in administrative orders. [658 D-G, 659 A-B; 768 F-H, 769 A-B]

q: What is the basic structure doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati?
answer:
The basic structure doctrine, as articulated in the judgment of His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru versus State of Kerala, [1973] SUPP. 1 S.C.R. 1, holds that the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 cannot be used to destroy or alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. The court emphasized that while amendments can adapt the system to changing conditions, they cannot change the democratic government, secular character, or other foundational aspects of the Constitution.

[Excerpts from His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru versus State of Kerala, [1973] SUPP. 1 S.C.R. 1, pages 670-671]

q: What is the Vishaka case about?
answer: The Vishaka case, [VISHAKA AND ORS. versus STATE OF RAJASTHAN AND ORS., [1997] SUPP. 3 S.C.R. 404], held that gender equality includes protection from sexual harassment and the right to work with dignity, which are fundamental human rights. The court laid down guidelines for preventing and addressing sexual harassment in the workplace, emphasizing the significance of international conventions and norms in interpreting constitutional rights. [410-fCJ, 413-C-D]

q: Explain the Puttaswamy judgment on privacy.
answer: In the Puttaswamy judgment, the Supreme Court of India held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The Court overruled earlier judgments such as M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh, which had held that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution. The Court emphasized that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and is also a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. The judgment also drew on international precedents, including the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, to underscore the importance of privacy in a democratic society.

q: What did the court decide in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia about anticipatory bail?
answer: The Supreme Court of India in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia et al. versus State of Punjab, decided that the power to grant anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the CrPC is not limited to specific contingencies as summarized by the High Court. The Court held that this power should be left to the discretion of the Court concerned, depending on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. The Court emphasized that the validity of Section 438 must be examined by the test of fairness and reasonableness, which is implicit in Article 21. The Court also noted that judicial discretion in granting anticipatory bail should not be unduly restricted, as such restrictions could be violative of Article 21. The Court rejected the High Court's Full Bench's view that the power under Section 438 is of an extraordinary character and must be exercised sparingly in exceptional cases only, and that it does not authorize the grant of blanket anticipatory bail for offences not yet committed or with regard to accusations not yet levelled. [GURBAKSH SINGH SIBBIA ETC . versus STATE OF PUNJAB, [1980] 3 S.C.R. 383, p. 36]

q: What does AIR 1978 SC 597 hold?
answer: The Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi versus Union of India, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621, held that the procedure prescribed by the state for curtailing or taking away personal liberty under Article 21 must still meet a possible challenge under other provisions of the Constitution. The court also emphasized the importance of the principles of natural justice, particularly the rule of audi alteram partem, in administrative actions that affect personal liberty. [658 D-G, 659 A-B; 768 F-H, 769 A-B]

q: What is (1973) 4 SCC 225 about?
answer: [1973] 4 SCC 225, [1973] SUPP. 1 S.C.R. 1, is a Supreme Court of India decision in the case of His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru versus State of Kerala. The judgment discusses several constitutional amendments, including the Twenty-Fifth and Twenty-Ninth Amendments. It addresses the validity of these amendments and their impact on the fundamental rights under Articles 13, 19, and 31 of the Constitution. The court also considered the implications of these amendments on the legislative powers of the state and central governments. q: Tell me about the case reported at (1997) 6 SCC 241.
answer: The case reported at [1997] 6 SCC 241 is Vishaka and Ors. versus State of Rajasthan and Ors. decided on 13 August 1997. The Supreme Court of India laid down guidelines and norms for preventing and redressing sexual harassment at the workplace. The court held that until specific legislation is enacted, these guidelines would be treated as the law declared by the Supreme Court under Article 141 of the Constitution of India. [Vishaka and Ors. versus State of Rajasthan and Ors., [1997] 6 SCC 241, 414-B]

q: Which case is reported at [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621?
answer: The case reported at [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621 is Maneka Gandhi versus Union of India. [MANEKA GANDHI versus UNION OF INDIA, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621]

q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Minerva Mills v. Union of India?
answer:
In Minerva Mills Ltd. & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., the Supreme Court held that the procedure prescribed in Article 368(2) of the Constitution for amending certain fundamental features of the Constitution must be strictly followed. The Court also held that the word "on any ground" in Article 368(4) is of such wide amplitude that it would cover even a ground that the procedure prescribed in Article 368(2) and its proviso has not been followed. As a result, the Court declared that any amendment purported to be made without complying with the procedure prescribed in Article 368(2) and its proviso would be unconstitutional and void.

[MINERVA MILLS LTD. & ORS. v. UNION OF INDIA & ORS., [1981] 1 S.C.R. 206, p. 288E-F]

q: What was decided in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain?
answer: In the case of Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the Supreme Court of India dismissed the petition challenging the disqualification of Indira Nehru Gandhi on the grounds that the disqualification was imposed on unconstitutional grounds, thereby affecting her fundamental rights. The court held that the disqualification by the House was not open to judicial review, distinguishing it from cases involving election disputes. [SMT. INDIRA NEHRU GANDHI versus SHRI RAJ NARAIN, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 347, p. 65]

q: What did the court say in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab?
answer:
In the case of I. C. Golak Nath & ORS. versus STATE OF PUNJAB & ANRS., the Supreme Court of India held that fundamental rights are primordial and given a transcendental position under the Constitution, and are kept beyond the reach of Parliament. The Court also stated that while the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution is derived from Articles 245, 246, and 248, it does not necessarily mean that every law made under Article 248 would be inconsistent with the articles sought to be amended. The Court rejected the argument that the continuance of the Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 was a gross violation of power.

[Excerpts from I. C. Golak Nath & ORS. versus STATE OF PUNJAB & ANRS., [1967] 2 S.C.R. 762, pages 789, 793, 794, 182]
